A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dynamic-vocabulary speculative-decoding work, renamed from MicroSpec to NanoSpec. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original throughput, acceptance-length, drafting-time, ablation and sensitivity results in Section 4 and Appendices A.2–A.3, although some comparator results are attributed to other papers.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds EAGLE-3 evaluations, component-level latency measurements and vocabulary-evolution analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.4.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same prompt/top-K initialization, draft and verification candidates, sliding-window deduplication, asynchronous gathering and GPU-resident state. The stream equations are reindexed and eviction terminology clarified. EAGLE-3 supplies an additional evaluation backbone without changing the proposed pruning procedure.

E1.justification: Evaluation coverage remains the six SpecBench tasks plus HumanEval code generation. The limited addition is ShareGPT training data for the reimplemented DynaSpec router in v2 Section 4.1; the additional backbone evaluations do not introduce new test tasks or domains.

E2.justification: v2 adds full-vocabulary EAGLE-3 comparisons in Tables 1 and 3 and removes CORAL from the main comparisons, Figure 3 and the Qwen appendix table. It also evaluates a reimplemented DynaSpec router for the Llama comparisons, while the Qwen DynaSpec results remain literature-reported. These changes materially reshape the comparison suite.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported 8B target from Llama-3-8B to Llama-3.1-8B and the GPU from H20Z to H20; the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun. v2 introduces EAGLE-3 evaluations using self-trained full-vocabulary draft heads, local DynaSpec training and CUDA-event latency profiling. Greedy decoding, the 1024-token limit and existing pruning hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the analyses with component-level latency profiling (Table 4), memory overhead accounting (Table 6), source-specific coverage and acceptance measurements (Table 8), and vocabulary-size/coverage trajectories during decoding (Figure 6). These examine computational bottlenecks and how vocabulary sources contribute over time. The original component ablation, Qwen analysis and window-size sensitivity study remain.

E5.justification: Table 2 newly states that speeds are averaged over three runs; v1 supplies no corresponding run count. Figure 6 specifies means and min–max ranges across samples. The existing Figure 4 error-bar practice is retained, and the new disclosure does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds EAGLE-3 results, including NanoSpec speeds of 430.0 and 944.8 tokens/s in Table 3, alongside new latency, memory and vocabulary-coverage results. Table 2 replaces DynaSpec averages of 378.1/799.2 with 367.7/762.8 tokens/s and supplies the previously missing 1B acceptance length of 2.92; CORAL entries disappear. These are added or replaced findings under revised reported settings, not demonstrated same-setting performance improvements between versions.

T1.justification: The candidate-stream and sliding-window definitions retain their mathematical substance. v2 explicitly writes the throughput formula for the existing oracle scenario and clarifies batching and bounded-memory costs, but these explain the existing construction. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims of training-free, lossless dynamic pruning with fewer than 3k active tokens remain. The contribution list revises the EAGLE-2 speedup range from 1.12–1.32× to 1.17–1.29× and adds a 1.19–1.28× EAGLE-3 claim. The conclusion correspondingly extends the demonstrated scope to multiple speculative-decoding algorithms.

C2.justification: The new Discussion identifies diminishing benefits for verification-dominated 70B+ models and discusses serving-framework integration. Section 4.2 adds a softmax noise-filtering explanation for acceptance behavior, while Appendix A.4 interprets source complementarity, vocabulary saturation and short-code-generation warm-up costs. These substantially expand mechanism explanations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and specifies the DynaSpec reimplementation: an 8.6M-parameter MLP, 256 spherical K-Means clusters and ShareGPT training. It discloses the need to train full-vocabulary EAGLE-3 drafts and adds CUDA-event profiling information, buffer names/sizes and FP16 memory-accounting parameters. These materially expand reproducibility information, although detailed EAGLE-3 training settings remain unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to EAGLE-3, PagedAttention and SGLang and positions the method as complementary to serving optimizations. A dedicated speculative-decoding vocabulary-pruning paragraph makes an explicit 'first fully dynamic, context-aware and training-free' claim, while largely retaining the frequency-based versus router-based distinction already present in v1. CORAL remains cited despite its removal from experiments.

P1.justification: The method/title is renamed, the abstract is rewritten, several evaluation passages are condensed or reorganized, and affiliations and publication information are updated. v2 adds a Discussion section and Appendix A.4, while retaining the main narrative sequence and most motivation, methodology and existing appendix exposition.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned with separate EAGLE-2/EAGLE-3 column groups. v2 adds four tables and the fourteen-panel Figure 6, removes CORAL rows and traces, and rearranges the main results displays. The original ablation and Qwen tables are retained as Tables 5 and 7, respectively; Figure 5 is resized rather than a new sensitivity result.

improvement.justification: The EAGLE-3 comparisons and component-level profiling strengthen evidence for compatibility and the source of speedups, while implementation disclosures and explicit scaling limitations improve transparency. The gain is tempered by removal of CORAL comparisons and new interpretive inconsistencies: Appendix A.4 claims coverage above 90% throughout decoding and RAG vocabulary below 1000, whereas Figure 6 shows otherwise. Overall, the added support provides a limited net improvement.
